bio_ocra.4.1.summary: The cell cycle is a series of carefully controlled stages in which a eukaryotic cell grows, replicates its genetic material, and divides to produce two genetically identical daughter cells via mitosis. This process is essential for organismal growth, repair of damaged tissues, and asexual reproduction. Through practical investigations like the root tip squash (PAG B1), students observe and calculate the mitotic index to understand how rapidly cells are dividing in meristematic regions.

core.p: The cell cycle is the regulated sequence of growth and division that all somatic cells undergo. It ensures that every new cell receives an exact copy of the parent cell's DNA, maintaining diploid chromosome numbers in human cells (46 chromosomes, or 23 pairs). Understanding this cycle explains how a single fertilized egg develops into a complex multicellular organism.
bullets: Divided into two main phases: Interphase and Cell Division (Mitosis and Cytokinesis).
Interphase takes up the vast majority of the cell cycle time.
Crucial checkpoints exist before DNA replication and mitosis to check for DNA damage.
Disruption of cell cycle controls can lead to uncontrolled cell division and tumor formation (cancer).

callouts.p: The cell cycle produces two genetically identical daughter cells for growth, tissue repair, and replacement.

core.p: Interphase is the active preparation phase before a cell divides. Although chromosomes are not yet visible under a light microscope because they are uncoiled as chromatin, intense metabolic activity is occurring inside the cell to synthesize proteins and organelles.
bullets: Gap 1 (G1): Cell grows larger, synthesizes new proteins, and replicates organelles.
Synthesis (S phase): DNA replication occurs, forming identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere.
Gap 2 (G2): Further growth, final protein synthesis, and checking of replicated DNA for errors.
Metabolic rate is extremely high throughout all three stages of interphase.

callouts.p: One of the two identical halves of a chromosome resulting from DNA replication.

core.p: Mitosis is nuclear division that produces two genetically identical daughter nuclei, each containing the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell. It is subdivided into four continuous stages: Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, and Telophase (mnemonic: PMAT).
bullets: Ensures genetic stability across generations of cell divisions.
Occurs in all somatic (body) cells.
Preceded by interphase and followed immediately by cytokinesis.
Chromosomes change from invisible chromatin threads to highly condensed, visible structures.

core.p: During prophase, the chromatin inside the nucleus condenses and coils tightly, making the chromosomes visible under a light microscope as two sister chromatids joined by a centromere. The nuclear envelope begins to break down, and spindle fibres start to form from the centrioles (in animal cells) or microtubule organizing centres.
bullets: Chromosomes condense and become shorter and thicker.
Nuclear membrane / envelope disintegrates.
Spindle apparatus begins to assemble across the cell.
Nucleolus disappears from view.

callouts.p: Look for dark, thickened threads inside a cell where the nuclear boundary is starting to fade.

core.p: In metaphase, the nuclear envelope has completely broken down. Spindle fibres attach to the centromere of each chromosome, pulling and guiding them so that they line up single file along the equator (metaphase plate) of the cell.
bullets: Chromosomes align along the cell equator (metaphase plate).
Spindle fibres attach firmly to each centromere.
Checkpoint ensures all chromosomes are properly attached before separation.

fig.cap: Metaphase: Chromosomes lined up along the equator with spindle fibres attached.

core.p: Anaphase is a rapid stage where the centromeres divide, splitting the sister chromatids apart. The spindle fibres shorten and contract, pulling the individual chromatids (now referred to as daughter chromosomes) toward opposite poles of the cell.
bullets: Centromeres split into two.
Sister chromatids are pulled apart to opposite poles.
Requires energy (ATP) provided by cellular respiration.
Chromosomes appear V-shaped as they are dragged through the cytoplasm.

callouts.p: Anaphase relies on ATP to power the motor proteins that move chromosomes along spindle fibres.

core.p: Once the chromosomes reach the opposite poles, telophase reverses the changes seen in prophase. The chromosomes uncoil back into long, thin chromatin strands, and a new nuclear envelope forms around each of the two new sets of chromosomes, creating two distinct nuclei.
bullets: Two new nuclear membranes form around the separated sets of chromosomes.
Chromosomes uncoil and become less distinct (chromatin).
Spindle fibres break down and disappear.
Nucleoli reappear in both new nuclei.

core.p: Cytokinesis is the physical division of the cytoplasm and cell membrane, completing cell division. In animal cells, the cell membrane pinches inward to form a cleavage furrow until the cell splits. In plant cells, a cell plate forms across the equator, which eventually develops into a new cell wall separating the two daughter cells.
bullets: Occurs immediately after or concurrently with telophase.
Animal cells: cleavage furrow pinches the cell in two.
Plant cells: vesicles fuse to form a cell plate and new cell wall.
Results in two genetically identical daughter cells.

core.h: 9. Required Practical: Root Tip Squash (PAG B1)
core.p: To study mitosis in plant cells, biologists use the root tip squash technique. The meristematic tissue at the very tip of a growing root (such as garlic or onion) is the active site of cell division. Roots are treated with acid and stained so chromosomes can be visualized under a light microscope.
bullets: Step 1: Grow roots on garlic bulbs in water for a few days.
Step 2: Cut off the last 1-2 mm of the root tip (where meristem is located).
Step 3: Treat with hydrochloric acid to break down pectin and break apart cell walls.
Step 4: Stain with toluidine blue or acetic orcein to stain chromosomes dark blue/red.
Step 5: Squash the root tip firmly on a microscope slide under a coverslip to create a single cell layer.

callouts.p: Do not slide the coverslip sideways when squashing, or you will break the chromosomes and ruin the slide view.

fig.cap: Root tip squash setup showing meristematic tissue location and slide preparation.

core.p: The mitotic index is a quantitative measure of cell proliferation, calculated as the ratio of cells undergoing mitosis to the total number of cells in a given field of view. It is widely used in cancer research and plant biology to assess growth rates.
bullets: Formula: Mitotic Index = (Number of cells with visible chromosomes / Total number of cells observed).
Can be expressed as a decimal or percentage.
Higher mitotic index indicates rapid cell division (e.g., cancer or active meristems).
Lower mitotic index indicates cells in resting or differentiated states.

callouts.p: Mitotic Index = Number of cells in mitosis / Total number of cells

core.h: 11. Significance of Mitosis in Multicellular Organisms
core.p: Mitosis is fundamental for life. Without it, multicellular organisms could neither grow from a zygote nor maintain their physical structure against everyday wear and tear.
bullets: Growth: Increases cell number in developing organisms.
Repair: Replaces damaged or dead cells (e.g., skin cells, gut lining).
Asexual reproduction: Produces genetically identical offspring in organisms like yeast, hydra, and many plants.
Genetic constancy: Ensures every cell has the exact same genetic instructions.

analogy.p: Imagine a high-tech factory printing identical instruction manuals. Interphase is the preparation and double-checking of the original master copy (S phase duplicating the master). Mitosis is the meticulous sorting of the two copies into separate piles on opposite sides of the factory floor (Prophase to Telophase), and cytokinesis is building a brand new wall right down the middle of the factory to create two independent, fully functioning duplicate factories. Where the analogy breaks down: cells are self-repairing and autonomous, whereas factory machines require human operators and external power.

terms.d: The regular sequence of growth, DNA replication, and division in cells.
The longest phase of the cell cycle where the cell grows, carries out normal metabolic functions, and replicates its DNA.
A type of nuclear division that produces two genetically identical daughter nuclei with the same number of chromosomes.
The uncoiled, spread-out form of DNA found in the nucleus during interphase.
A tightly coiled structure of DNA and histone proteins visible during cell division.
One of two identical strands of a replicated chromosome joined by a centromere.
The region where two sister chromatids are joined together and where spindle fibres attach.
Microtubules that form during mitosis to pull chromosomes apart.
The central plane of a dividing cell where chromosomes align during metaphase.
The division of the cytoplasm and cell membrane following nuclear division.
A region of plant tissue found at growing tips where cells actively divide by mitosis.
The ratio of cells in mitosis to the total number of cells observed in a sample.
An indentation of the cell membrane in animal cells that deepens during cytokinesis to pinch the cell in two.
A structure that forms across the equator of a dividing plant cell, precursor to the new cell wall.

mistakes.r: Mitosis is specifically nuclear division; cell division includes both mitosis and cytokinesis.

mistakes.w: Stating DNA replication happens during mitosis.
mistakes.r: DNA replication occurs in the S phase of interphase, before mitosis begins.

mistakes.w: Forgetting why acid is used in root tip squash.
mistakes.r: Acid breaks down pectin between plant cell walls so cells can be squashed into a single layer.

mistakes.w: Claiming plant cells form a cleavage furrow.
mistakes.r: Plant cells have a rigid cell wall so they form a cell plate instead.
Chromatin is loose and uncoiled during interphase; chromosomes are condensed and visible during mitosis.
Mitotic index is (cells in mitosis / total cells), not total cells divided by cells in mitosis.

mistakes.w: Saying daughter cells are genetically different.
mistakes.r: Mitosis produces genetically identical daughter cells (clones).

exam.q: State the purpose of mitosis in a multicellular organism.
model: Repair of damaged tissues / replacement of cells
exam.tip: Always give two distinct uses unless the question specifies a single function.

exam.q: Describe what happens to chromosomes during metaphase.
model: Chromosomes line up along the equator (metaphase plate) of the cell
Spindle fibres attach to the centromeres
exam.tip: Mention both the alignment position and the spindle fibre attachment.

exam.q: Explain why the S phase of interphase is crucial before a cell undergoes mitosis.
model: DNA is replicated / copied during S phase
Ensures each daughter cell receives an identical and complete set of genetic information
exam.tip: Link replication to genetic consistency in daughter cells.

exam.q: A student counts 45 cells undergoing mitosis in a total field of view containing 200 cells. Calculate the mitotic index.
exam.tip: Show your fraction clearly. State units if asked (percentage or decimal).

exam.q: Describe how cytokinesis differs between plant and animal cells.
model: Animal cells form a cleavage furrow that pinches the cell membrane inward
Plant cells cannot pinch due to the rigid cell wall
Plant cells instead form a cell plate across the equator which becomes a new cell wall
exam.tip: Contrasting structure (rigid wall vs flexible membrane) explains the difference in mechanism.

exam.q: Explain the role of hydrochloric acid in the root tip squash practical.
model: Allows cells to be easily separated into a single layer on the slide
exam.tip: Do not just say 'softens the root'; name pectin or cell separation.

exam.q: Name the stage of the cell cycle where DNA replication occurs.
exam.tip: Be precise: just writing 'interphase' is often too broad if the mark scheme asks for the specific sub-phase.

exam.q: Describe the events that occur during anaphase of mitosis.
model: Centromeres divide and sister chromatids are pulled apart
Chromatids move toward opposite poles of the cell
exam.tip: Mention centromere splitting and movement to poles.

exam.q: Explain why root tips are used when observing mitosis under a light microscope.
model: Cells in the meristem are actively dividing by mitosis
exam.tip: Use the biological term 'meristem' to guarantee full marks.

worked.q: A student observes a slide of an onion root tip and counts a total of 350 cells. Of these, 77 cells are clearly showing stages of mitosis. Calculate the mitotic index for this tissue sample.
steps: Identify the formula for mitotic index: Mitotic Index = (Number of cells in mitosis) / (Total number of cells)
Substitute the values into the formula: 77 / 350
Convert to a percentage if required: 0.22 × 100 = 22%

worked.q: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes in its nucleus at the start of interphase. State how many chromosomes and how many DNA molecules are present in the cell during (a) G2 phase, and (b) immediately after anaphase.
steps: Understand that in G2, DNA has replicated so each chromosome consists of 2 sister chromatids joined at a centromere.
(a) Chromosome number remains 46 (counted by centromeres), but there are 92 DNA molecules.
Understand that in anaphase, sister chromatids separate, becoming individual chromosomes moving to opposite poles.
(b) Chromosome number temporarily becomes 92 (until cytokinesis divides them into two cells of 46 each), and there are 92 DNA molecules.
worked.ans: (a) 46 chromosomes, 92 DNA molecules; (b) 92 chromosomes, 92 DNA molecules.
